name: Hernan Diaz
one_line: An Argentine-born, Sweden-raised, English-adopting novelist (correctly Hernan Diaz, not "Herman") who writes elegantly cold, formally rigged fictions about the two things American literature has been least honest about: the emptiness of the frontier and the machinery of money.
bio: Diaz was born in Buenos Aires in 1973; his family fled to Sweden when he was about two, after the 1976 military coup, and returned to Argentina roughly seven years later when democracy was restored — an exile that left him permanently between languages and countries. He studied literature at the University of Buenos Aires and King's College London before moving to New York for a PhD in comparative literature at NYU, and spent years as a scholar and editor, serving as associate director of the Hispanic Institute at Columbia and publishing an academic monograph, 'Borges, between History and Eternity' (2012). His fiction career started late and from the margins: 'In the Distance' (2017) was turned down widely before the small nonprofit Coffee House Press took it, whereupon it became a Pulitzer finalist, a PEN/Faulkner finalist and a Saroyan Prize winner. 'Trust' (2022) made him a mainstream literary figure — Kirkus Prize, Booker longlist, a shared Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2023, an HBO adaptation in development, and a place on the NYT's best-books-of-the-century list; a further novel ('Preston Bound') has been announced.
known_for: 'In the Distance' (2017) — an anti-Western about a Swedish immigrant, Håkan Söderström, walking east against the tide of settlers; a frontier stripped of heroism, dialogue and speed
'Trust' (2022) — four nested, competing documents (a novel, an unfinished memoir, a ghostwriter's recollection, a wife's diary) about a Wall Street financier and the woman written out of his story
Winning the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction (shared with Barbara Kingsolver's 'Demon Copperhead')
'Borges, between History and Eternity' (2012), his scholarly book on Borges
The argument that money is both the dominant force in modern life and a literary taboo — and that fiction has almost never depicted money being made
Reviving and estranging genre: the Western, the financial saga, the memoir, the diary, used as forms to be dismantled from inside
school: No school in the doctrinal sense. He sits at the crossroads of Borgesian metafiction, the Latin American 'literature about literature' tradition, and a modernist-formalist lineage (Stein, Beckett, Bernhard) applied to American historical material — plus a scholar's toolkit of narratology and critical theory used quietly rather than displayed.
lineage: He is explicit that Borges is foundational ('I wouldn't be the person I am without Borges'), and behind Borges the puzzle-makers of nested and unreliable narration; he draws on Melville, Henry James, Willa Cather and Gertrude Stein for American form and sentence, and on Beckett and Thomas Bernhard for reduction and voice. His revisionist frontier owes something to Cormac McCarthy and the anti-mythic Western while pointedly refusing McCarthy's violence-as-grandeur. Downstream, he has become a reference point for the current wave of documentary/polyphonic novels about capital and archival silence, and for a broader literary turn toward finance as subject matter.
stance: Literature does not passively reflect reality; it helps manufacture it — and the most powerful fictions in modern life are the ones we don't call fiction. Money is the clearest case: a shared convention with no substance, which nonetheless reshapes the world, and whose narratives are written by winners who then pass their version off as history. So form is an ethical matter, not decoration: how a narrative distributes and withholds knowledge, and whose voice gets to sound authoritative, is where the politics of a book actually live. His two novels attack what he calls blind spots in the American canon — the frontier's tedium, slowness and immigrant bewilderment rather than its glamorized conquest, and the erasure of women from every story about the accumulation of capital.
blind_spots: The most persistent criticism is temperature: his books are admired for architecture and prose control while being described as chilly, cerebral and short on interiority — characters serving as positions in a structure rather than people, with 'Trust' only fully warming when Ida Partenza speaks. Sceptics also see the metafictional apparatus as a somewhat schematic delivery system: once you grasp that each document is lying, the reveal is more satisfying as design than as surprise, and the feminist inversion (the genius was the wife) is a neat reversal that some find morally tidy. 'In the Distance' draws the charge of picaresque drift and a near-mute, passive protagonist, and although it refuses frontier heroics, Indigenous characters remain largely peripheral to a European immigrant's consciousness. And his critique of capital is diagnostic rather than programmatic — it dismantles the myths without committing to an alternative, which readers wanting real political heat find evasive.
politics: Discernible in outline, deliberately unspecific in party terms. His formative fact is political — a family that fled Argentina's 1976 dictatorship — and his fiction is unmistakably left-of-centre in its preoccupations: the fictitiousness and violence of speculative capital, class as a subject American literature has suppressed, the erasure of women from economic history, and the frontier myth as propaganda. In interviews he frames these as literary and ethical problems rather than a platform, and he does not present himself as an activist or align publicly with candidates or movements in any sustained way; he has also resisted reducing 'Trust' to a topical allegory about any particular oligarch or administration. Fair summary: culturally progressive and structurally anti-plutocratic in sensibility, with no clearly documented partisan affiliation — anything more specific would be guesswork.
public_views: Money is simultaneously the force that shapes our lives and a taboo subject; fiction almost always begins after the fortune has been made
Women have been essentially erased from narratives about the accumulation of capital, and that erasure is itself a story worth telling
Money is a fiction — a convention we've all been compelled to accept — which is precisely why it belongs in the hands of novelists
There is a moral dimension to how a narrative administers knowledge; withholding and revealing are ethical acts, not just tricks
He wants fiction that takes the reader seriously: clues planted early, conventions challenged, no condescension
Power routinely blurs the line between fiction and truth, and rewrites history in its own favour
The American canon glamorizes westward expansion; the reality was slow, empty, bureaucratic and largely inglorious
English is an adopted home rather than an inheritance; foreignness and accent are conditions he writes from, not obstacles he overcame
Genre is a set of conventions that can be inhabited in order to be estranged
Borges is constitutive of who he is as a reader and writer
He drafts longhand with a fountain pen, and treats the archive — ledgers, memoirs, financial documents — as raw literary material
interview_notes: Precise, courteous and unhurried, with a professor's habit of reframing a question into a better one before answering it. He is more comfortable discussing form, archives and the history of the novel than his own psychology, and tends to redirect biographical questions toward craft — which reads as elegant to some interviewers and as guarded to others. Recurring themes: money as taboo, the ethics of narrative form, foreignness and language, genre as convention, Borges, and the archival research behind his books. Dry, self-deprecating humour surfaces regularly (the disorientation of prize stickers, the absurdity of a novelist of capital who writes by hand), and he is notably generous about small presses and translators.
personal: Exile is the organizing fact of his life: born in Buenos Aires, uprooted to Sweden as a toddler by the 1976 coup, repatriated as a child, then educated across Argentina, London and New York. He is a trained comparatist (PhD, NYU) who worked for years in academia and editing — including as associate director of Columbia's Hispanic Institute — and came to novel-writing in his forties, with 'In the Distance' arriving via a small nonprofit publisher after wide rejection. That Swedish childhood surfaces directly in the Swedish protagonist of 'In the Distance', and the experience of writing in a third or fourth language underwrites his interest in characters who cannot make themselves understood.
key_topics: speculative capital and finance in fiction
the erasure of women from economic history
class in the American literary canon
the relationship between fiction, history and power
